6477.t: CE6430: Advances in Remote Sensing and GIS
6477.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE6430 : Advances in Remote Sensing and GIS { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Mechanism of Remote sensing, Ideal Remote Sensing System, Elements of Remote Sensing System, Passive and Active Remote Sensing, Electromagnetic radiations, Electromagnetic Spectrum, Interaction with the atmosphere, Energy sources and radiation principle, scattering, absorption, atmospheric windows, Interaction with targets, albedo, spectral reflectance curves of earth features, Characteristics of images. [10 hrs]
Module II: Satellite characteristics-Orbits, Swath, Nadir, Pixel size, Sensor resolutions- Spatial, Spectral, Radiometric and Temporal. Indian Satellites and other purpose driven satellites, Data products. [8 hrs]
Module III: Image interpretation, Image processing techniques, Optical and infra-red Remote sensing, Thermal remote sensing, Microwave remote sensing, Hyperspectral remote sensing, Basics of Radar, Digital image processing system, Pre-processing of raw data, Image enhancement, Transformation, Supervised and un-supervised Classification, Accuracy assessment, Data Integration, analysis and interpretation. [10 hrs]
Module IV: Introduction to GIS, GIS components, Data sources and products, Spatial reference system and geo-referencing, Projection system, Data acquisition- raster and vector data, Registration and relating different data, Spatial analysis, Data integration, Data modeling, Data models, Data structures, Measurement of length, perimeter and area, management, Database models, Geospatial analysis, Spatial statistics, Database query, Reclassification, Buffering, Overlaying of Maps, Spatial interpolation, Surface analysis, Network analysis, Principal Component analysis, applications of GIS. [12 hrs]

Course Objective

1 .

To enable the students to improve their understanding regarding data acquisition through remote sensing.
2 .

To empower the students with skills in managing spatial data in digital format
3 .

To develop understanding regarding principles and technics for image analysis
4 .

To apply the knowledge gained for solving problems related to water resources

Course Outcome

1 .

On completion of the course, the student should be capable
CO1: To understand the scope of Remote Sensing and GIS
CO2: To develop understanding about satellite data products and their uses
CO3: To work with various image processing techniques
CO4: To gain exposure towards geospatial tools
CO5: To understand the utility of remote sensing and GIS for analyzing earth surface features

Essential Reading

1 .

T. M. Lillesand, R. W. Kiefer, J. W. Chipman, Remote Sensing and Image Interpretation, Willey

2 .

A. M. Chandra and S. K. Ghosh, Remote Sensing and Geographical Information System, Narosa Publishing House

Supplementary Reading

1 .

George Joseph, Fundamentals of Remote Sensing, Universities Press

2 .

J.A. Richards, Remote Sensing Digital Image Analysis, Springer

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CR6172 : Advanced Ceramic Processing Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Experiment 1: Shear-thinning and shear-thickening behavior of the slurry: Requirements: Clay, quartz, bauxite powder, DI water, Darvan C, NaSiO3, measuring cylinders, 100 mL pots, porcelain balls, rheometer. 3 Hours
Experiment 2: Determination of particle size and particle size distribution by Andreasen pipette method: Requirements: Ball clay, China clay, Darvan C, Andreasen pipette, weighing machine, hot air oven, Petri dish, glass stirrer, DI water. 3 Hours
Experiment 3: Compaction behavior of clay-based (Triaxial body) ceramics and determination of agglomeration breakpoint: Requirements: Ball/China clay, quartz, feldspar, PVA, weighing machine, DI water, hydraulic press, die (25 mm diameter). 3 Hours
Experiment 4: Effect of grinding on the alpha to beta quartz transformation behavior using DSC-XRD analysis: Requirements: Quartz powder, capped pot, porcelain ball, planetary mill, Particle size analyzer, beaker, ultrasonicator, DI water, TG-DSC apparatus, XRD apparatus. 3 Hours
Experiment 5: Drying behavior of clay-sand mixture with different moisture level: Requirements: China/Ball clay, DI water, knife/blade, measuring scale/ruler, drying oven, wet cloth, weighing balance, small tray (4 pc), transparent glass sheets. 3 Hours
Experiment 6: Effect of binder content on apparent porosity, bulk density, and green strength (CCS, DTS): Requirements: China/Ball clay, quartz, PVA, DI water, hydraulic press, die, weighing balance, vacuum pump, AP measurement setup. 3 Hours
Experiment 7: Rheological behavior and optimization of deflocculant concentration for a stable slip preparation: Requirements: China clay, DI water, deflocculant (Darvan C, NaSiO3, Na2CO3, STP, etc.) graduated cylinders (6 pc), planetary mill, capped pot, porcelain ball, aluminum foil, weighing balance, stirring rod. 3 Hours
Experiment 8: Preparation and characterization of MgAl2O4 spinel by citrate-nitrate route: Requirements: Mg and Al-nitrate salt, citric acid, DI water, EG/PEG, beakers, hot plate, weighing balance, petri dish, pH meter, pH paper, drying oven, XRD/SEM apparatus. 3 Hours
Experiment 9: Measurement of the diametral tensile strength and the flexural strength of fired clay and triaxial bodies: Requirements: China/Ball clay, quartz, feldspar, Vernier calipers, drying oven, 1200ºC box furnace, Instron UTM, XRD. 3 Hours
Experiment 10: Slip casting of a clay-based body and establishing the relationship between thickness cast and casting time: Requirements: China/Ball clay, sieve, beaker, graduated cylinder, Vernier calipers, Plaster of Paris mold, Darvan C, PVA, stearic acid. 3 Hours
Experiment 11: Determination of plastic limit and liquid limit from Atterberg plasticity index: Requirements: China/Ball clay, quartz, feldspar, sieve, glass stirring rod, petridish, beaker, graduated cylinder, Darvan C, PVA, stearic acid. 3 Hours
Experiment 12: Deformation behavior of a plastic clay/triaxial body using Pfefferkorn plasticity tester: Requirements: China/Ball clay, quartz, feldspar, sieve, beaker, graduated cylinder, glass stirring rod, petridish, Darvan C, PVA, stearic acid. 3 Hours

Course Objective

1 .

To provide hands-on experience in various ceramic processing routes.
2 .

To impart and develop a fundamental understanding of ceramic part processing and fabrication phenomena at the postgraduate level for ceramic engineering students.
3 .

Develop prototype finished products using clay-based traditional ceramics and understand how different process parameters control microstructure and properties.

Course Outcome

1 .

Apply theoretical knowledge to independently synthesize ceramic materials in bulk, porous, and powder forms.
2 .

Analyze industrial ceramic processing phenomena and develop prototype products at the laboratory scale.
3 .

Demonstrate hands-on proficiency in advanced ceramic processing techniques at the laboratory scale.
4 .

Design conventional and advanced ceramic products at the laboratory scale to address emerging technological needs.
5 .

Implement ceramic fabrication methods, perform analytical characterization, and effectively document and present results within stipulated timelines.

Essential Reading

1 .

P Saha, Laboratory Manual for Advanced Ceramic Processing Laboratory, In house , Provided during Laboratory

Supplementary Reading

1 .

James S Reed, Principles of Ceramic Fabrication, John Wiley & Sons , textbook

2 .

M.N. Rahman, Ceramic Processing & Sintering, Marcel Dekker Inc , textbook

Journal and Conferences

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CY4301 : Quantum Chemistry { 3-1-0 / 4}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Invalid assumptions of classical mechanics, Black body radiation, Planck’s quantum theory, Photoelectric effect, molar heat capacity of monoatomic solids, Atomic spectra, Bohr theory of atom, Angular momentum, wave – particle duality, de Broglie equation, Heisenberg uncertainty principle, The wave equation, postulates of quantum mechanics and Schrodinger equation, Operators and commutation relations, Hermitian nature of operator, expectation values, Application of quantum postulates to simple model systems (particle in 1D, 2D and 3D box, Harmonic oscillator, Rotation in 2 and 3 dimensions), Hydrogen atom, Radial and angular wavefunctions, Angular momentum, vector model, Total wavefunctions and orbital presentations, Approximation methods: Time-independent perturbation theory, Variation method-secular determinants and secular equations, Hartree-Fock equations, self-consistent field method, atoms and molecules, bonding and application to spectroscopy.

Course Objective

1 .

The course is designed to provide an overview of the quantum chemical description of atoms and molecules, their reactivity and chemical bonding.
2 .

To provide knowledge on solving Schrodinger equation on simpler systems.
3 .

To provide knowledge on approximation methods.
4 .

To instill the concept of quantum chemistry's application in atoms and molecules.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Students will be able to gain an overview of the quantum chemical description of atoms and molecules, their reactivity and chemical bonding.
2. Students will be able to gain knowledge on solving Schrodinger equation on simpler systems.
3. Students will be able to gain knowledge on approximation methods.
4. The concept of quantum chemistry's application in atoms and molecules is expected to be instilled in students' minnd

Essential Reading

1 .

Donald A. McQuarrie, Quantum Chemistry, University Science Books , Indian Edition: Viva Books Pvt Ltd. 2003

2 .

Ira N. Levine, Quantum chemistry, Pearson Education , Fifth edition

Supplementary Reading

1 .

P. W. Atkins, R. S. Friedman, Ronald Friedman, Molecular Quantum Mechanics, Oxford University Press , 4th edition

2 .

R. K. Prasad, Quantum Chemistry, New Age International Publishers , 1996

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ER5071 : Geochemistry Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

1. Identification of standard mineral using X-ray Diffraction Method (XRD).
2. Identification of crystal structure by X-ray Diffraction Method (XRD).

4. Determination of chemical index of alteration (CIA).

To train the students on the fundamentals concept of geochemistry, and practical application through different approaches

CO1: To determine the mineralogy using advanced technique
CO2: To understand the methods for calculation of different geochemical parameters
CO3: To understand the fundamentals of the activity-activity plots
CO4: To understand the fundamentals of the Eh-pH plots

7757.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : HS1344 : Financial Market and Institutions { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Modules:
1, Introduction of financial System- financial system and economy, Reforms in the financial system, Role of Indian financial system-structure of financial system, nature and role of financial system.
2. Financial Markets - the place of financial markets in the economy-real assets and financial assets, money market, capital market, primary market, secondary market, government securities market, foreign exchange market, debt market, and derivative market.
3. Development of Financial Institution and Instrument- new financial instrument, evolution of development bank, changing role of development financial institution, banking and non banking institution, Commercial banks, co-operative bank, mutual funds, insurance companies, and financial regulation.
4. Regulatory and Promotional Institutions- RBI, SEBI, the purpose of regulation, levels of regulations.
5. Non-Bank Financial Intermediaries and Statutory Financial Organization- Small saving, Provident funds, and pension funds
6. Foreign Capital Flows-Types of foreign capital Uses and determinants of foreign capital, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI),
Foreign Portfolio Investment.

Course Objective

1 .

The basic objective of the course is to provide comprehensive introduction to the functioning of financial market in the emerging context of deregulation and globalization of markets.

Course Outcome

1 .

The topics such as the Indian financial system, organized and nonorganized financial sector, capital market, derivative market, and market volatility are covered in this course to equip the student with tools and technical apparatus necessary to analyze modern literature on financial markets and financial institutions.

Essential Reading

1 .

L.M. Bhole, Financial Institutions and Markets: Structure, Growth and Innovation, Tata McGraw Hill Publishing Company Limited, New Delhi, 2009

2 .

Bharati. V. Pathak, Indian Financial System, Pearson Education in South Asia Publishing Company, New Delhi, 2006

Supplementary Reading

1 .

V.A Avadhani, Financial Economics: Theory and Practice, Financial Economics: Theory and Practice

2 .

H.J. Johnson, Financial Institutions and Markets, Tata McGraw Hill Publishing Company Limited, NY,1993

8781.t: FP3474: Livestock, Fish and Marine Products Laboratory
8781.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : FP3474 : Livestock, Fish and Marine Products Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Practical training in the processing and evaluation of livestock, fish, and marine products with hands-on experience in slaughtering, dressing, and preparing meat cuts from poultry, goat, and pig, as well as learning techniques for curing, chilling, freezing, and measuring meat tenderness. The egg quality assessment, pasteurization, and egg powder preparation. For fish and marine products, experiments on curing, freezing, drying, and canning. The application of scientific principles to ensure product quality, safety, and compliance with industry standards.

Course Objective

1 .

To provide students with practical skills in the slaughtering, dressing, and processing of livestock, fish, and marine products.
2 .

To familiarize students with methods for fish processing, including curing, freezing, drying, and canning.
3 .

To train students in assessing the quality of eggs and preparing egg-based products like pasteurized egg liquid and egg powder.
4 .

To emphasize the importance of quality control, safety, and compliance with industry standards.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Demonstrate proficiency in slaughtering, dressing, and preparing meat cuts from poultry, goat, and pig, and apply techniques for meat curing, chilling, freezing, and tenderness measurement.
2. Evaluate the external and internal quality of eggs and prepare egg-based products such as pasteurized egg liquid and egg powder.
3. Perform fish processing techniques, including curing, freezing, drying, and canning.
4. Analyze and implement quality control measures in the processing of livestock, fish, and marine products, while developing a comprehensive understanding of the scientific principles and standards governing these processes.

Essential Reading

1 .

R. A. Lawrie, Lawrie's Meat Science, Woodhead Publishing

2 .

Ioannis S. Boziaris, Seafood Processing: Technology, Quality and Safety, John Wiley & Sons, Ltd

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Yasmine Motarjemi and Huub Lelieveld, Food Safety Management: A Practical Guide for the Food Industry, Elsevier

2 .

Isabel Guerrero-Legarreta and Y. H. Hui, Handbook of Poultry Science and Technology, Wiley

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ME4136 : Robotics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Introduction to Robotics (5 Hours)
Introduction, Automation and Robotics, brief history, Social and economic aspects, Advantages overview of robots and future application.
Module 2: Analysis of direct & inverse kinematics, DH representation (9 Hours)
Classification & structure of robotic system: Classification, Configuration, wrist, end effectors , Links, Joints, Drive system. Robot Kinematics: Direct & inverse kinematics, rotation matrix, composite rotation matrix, homogenous transformations, links, joints DH representation, Geometrical approach of direct & reverse kinematics Robot Arm dynamics: Joint velocities, KE, PE & motion equation of manipulating trajectory planning, joint interpolated trajectory
Module 3: Sensors and actuators used in robotics system(8 Hours)
Description and Applications of various Sensors used for Robotic Systems. Types of electric, pneumatic and hydraulic actuator system used for robotic application,
Module 4: Control of robotics system(7 Hours)
Control System: Basic control system concepts, model, transformation and block diagrams, controllers ON & OFF, transient response,
Module 5: Robotic Programming Language and AI methods(7 Hours)
Robot Programming: Languages, Graphics, Storing & operating, Task programs. Description of Mobile Robots, Application of various Al methodology to control robots.

Course Objective

1 .

1. To understand the fundamental concepts and components of Robotics systems.
2 .

2. To study direct & inverse kinematics of robots.
3 .

3. To explore different types of sensors and actuators used in robotics applications.
4 .

4. To analyse control of robotics systems.
5. To study programming and artificial intelligence techniques for robotics systems.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able:
1. To explain the fundamental concepts and components of Robotics systems.
2. To explain direct & inverse kinematics of robots.
3. Identify and classify different types of sensors and actuators used in robotics applications.
4. To do control of robotics systems.
5. To deploy programming and artificial intelligence techniques for robotics systems.

Essential Reading

1 .

J.J.Craig, Introduction to Robotics, Pearson Education , 2022

2 .

Mordechai Ben-Ari , Francesco Mondada, Elements of Robotics, Kindle Edition, Publisher Springer , 2025

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Nicholas Odrey (Author), Mitchell Weiss (Author), Mikell Groover (Author), Roger Nagel (Author), Ashish Dutta (Author), Industrial Robotics -Technology ,Programming and Applications, Mc Graw-Hill , 2017

2 .

Damith Herath , David St-Onge, Foundations of Robotics: A Multidisciplinary Approach with Python and ROS, Kindle Edition, Springer Verlag, Singapore , 2025

7245.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : SM6402 : Operations and Project Management { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Introduction: Operations Function and its Applications, Operations Strategy & Competitiveness Current issues in Operations Management, Break Even Analysis for Multi Product Situations Quantitative Forecasting Models. Facility and Capacity Planning: Facility Layout and Location Models, Manufacturing and Service process Selection and Design, Principles and Types of Plant Layout, Strategic Capacity Planning, Matching Demand and Capacity (Aggregate planning). Employee Productivity: Process Analysis, Work System Design, Operations Scheduling, Time Study and Setting Standards, Maintenance Planning and Management. Projects and Project Management: Project Management Life Cycle and Uncertainty, The Project Management Process, Developing and Presenting the Project Plan, Setting up a Project Plan, Project Teams. Managing the Project: Project Planning and Implementation, Project Monitoring, Evaluation and Control, Project Cost Analysis, Managing Issues in Projects, Managing Risks.

Course Objective

1 .

To gain an understanding and appreciation of the principles and applications relevant to the
planning, design, and operations of manufacturing/service firms.
2 .

To gain some ability to recognize situations in a production system environment that suggests
the use of certain quantitative methods to assist in decision making on operations management
and strategy.
3 .

To understand the managerial responsibility for Operations, even when production is
outsourced, or performed in regions far from corporate headquarters.

Course Outcome

1 .

The course will equip students to understand the basic aspects and applications of Operations and Project Management to handle the hindrances in executing a project.

Essential Reading

Chase, R., Jacobs, F. R., Aquilano, N., & Agarwal, N., Operations Management for Competitive Advantage (11thed.)., The McGraw Hill

2 .
